findings.claim: Understanding this world is essential for the Eduqas exam because ...
findings.truth: House rule: lesson prose must never name the board. Use neutral wording ('the exam').
findings.evidence: House rule for Eduqas/WJEC lessons (neutral phrasing).

findings.claim: In the Eduqas Component 2 Section B exam, you will be given a printed extract ...
findings.truth: Board name plus a paper/section code, both banned. The real facts are: one source-based response on the novel, 40 marks, closed book.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2 Component 2, Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks); 'Learners are not permitted to take copies of the set texts into the examination.'

findings.claim: In the Eduqas exam, context (AO3) must be woven into analysis
findings.truth: Board must not be named in lesson prose.
findings.evidence: House rule.

findings.claim: Match item for Mr Bingley: 'Wealth from trade, recently acquired estate'
findings.truth: Bingley has acquired no estate. He inherited nearly a hundred thousand pounds; his father died before buying an estate and Bingley rents Netherfield as a tenant.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.4: 'Mr. Bingley inherited property to the amount of nearly a hundred thousand pounds from his father, who had intended to purchase an estate, but did not live to do it ... he was now established only as a tenant.'

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions across lessons 1-8 are labelled '20 marks - Extract Analysis' with a 20-mark ladder; lessons 4-8 use a malformed 'Band 4-1: Progressively less detailed' tail.
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose question is worth 40 marks. All 48 labels relabelled to 40 and every ladder rescaled to five equal house bands: Top (33-40), Upper-mid (25-32), Mid (17-24), Lower-mid (9-16), Low (1-8). 'Lower band' renamed 'Low band'.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2: 'Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks)'.

findings.claim: In Chapter 6, she tells Charlotte: 'I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.'
findings.truth: The line is in Chapter 5, in the Lucases' visit to Longbourn. Elizabeth is answering Miss Lucas (Charlotte), so the speaker and addressee are right; only the chapter is wrong.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.5: '"That is very true," replied Elizabeth, "and I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine."'

findings.claim: The Eduqas extract question may come from these early chapters.
findings.truth: Board must not be named in lesson prose.
findings.evidence: House rule.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Mrs Bennet ultimatum threatens Elizabeth after Collins's proposal?' - answer 'From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents.'
findings.truth: The line is Mr Bennet's, and it is a joke at Mrs Bennet's expense, not her ultimatum. The lesson body attributes it correctly; only the flashcard is wrong.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.20: '"An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents ..."' spoken by Mr Bennet.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Darcy phrase in his first proposal offends Elizabeth?' - answer 'Arrogance, conceit, and selfish disdain.'
findings.truth: These are Elizabeth's words condemning Darcy, not Darcy's words. A student quoting this as Darcy's own phrase would be wrong.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.34, Elizabeth: 'your manners impressing me with the fullest belief of your arrogance, your conceit, and your selfish disdain of the feelings of others'.

findings.claim: Pemberley's grounds are 'neither formally nor falsely adorned' (twice in content, plus the knowledge-check stem, a flashcard answer and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Austen writes 'neither formal nor falsely adorned' (of the stream's banks). 'formally' is a misquotation students would reproduce in the exam.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.43: 'Its banks were neither formal nor falsely adorned.'

findings.claim: He is 'eager to introduce his sister' to Elizabeth
findings.truth: Not a quotation from the novel. Darcy says 'Will you allow me ... to introduce my sister to your acquaintance'. The quotation marks are removed.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.44: 'who more particularly wishes to be known to you. Will you allow me, or do I ask too much, to introduce my sister to your acquaintance'.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: "'Gentleman-like' and eager to introduce his sister - versus proud and aloof."
findings.truth: 'gentleman-like' comes from Elizabeth's reproach at the first proposal, not from any description of Darcy at Pemberley.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.34: 'had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner.'

findings.claim: Lydia, the youngest Bennet sister at just fifteen, runs away with Wickham
findings.truth: Lydia is sixteen at the elopement. She is fifteen when first described early in the novel, but she turns sixteen in the June before the August elopement.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.49, Mrs Bennet: 'And she was only sixteen last June.' ch.41, Elizabeth: 'she will, at sixteen, be the most determined flirt'.

findings.claim: Elizabeth learns of the elopement while at Pemberley with the Gardiners
findings.truth: She is at the inn at Lambton when Jane's letters reach her; Darcy calls on her there. She is not at Pemberley.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.46 (the Lambton inn scene).

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Mrs Bennet line condemns Lydia's elopement?' - answer 'The death of your daughter would have been a blessing in comparison.'
findings.truth: The line is Mr Collins's, from his letter of condolence to Mr Bennet. The lesson body attributes it correctly; only the flashcard is wrong.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.48, Mr Collins's letter: 'The death of your daughter would have been a blessing in comparison of this.'

findings.claim: 'His affection for her soon sank into indifference' (content and the knowledge-check stem)
findings.truth: Austen writes 'sunk', not 'sank'.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.61: 'His affection for her soon sunk into indifference: hers lasted a little longer.'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Darcy line acknowledges his moral growth?' - answer 'Let me once in my life feel how much I have been to blame.'
findings.truth: The line is Mr Bennet's, admitting his failure as a father after the elopement. It has nothing to do with Darcy. The lesson body attributes it correctly.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.48, Mr Bennet to Elizabeth: 'No, Lizzy, let me once in my life feel how much I have been to blame.'

findings.claim: Fill stem: 'Elizabeth is described as having "a lively, _____ turn" of mind'
findings.truth: Austen writes 'a lively, playful disposition'. 'turn of mind' is not in the text, so the stem teaches a misquotation. The answer ('playful') is right.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.3: 'for she had a lively, playful disposition, which delighted in anything ridiculous.'

findings.claim: For character questions in the Eduqas exam, always link character to theme
findings.truth: Board must not be named in lesson prose.
findings.evidence: House rule.

findings.claim: the narrator reports that Darcy was 'discovered to be proud, to be above his company, and not at all to be liked'
findings.truth: Fabricated ending. Austen writes 'and above being pleased'. The invented clause sits inside a Key Fact box that tells students to memorise it.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.3: 'he was discovered to be proud, to be above his company, and above being pleased'.

findings.claim: when Elizabeth tells Jane that Darcy is 'the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry'
findings.truth: Elizabeth says this to Darcy himself, at the height of her refusal of his first proposal. Jane is not present.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.34: 'I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Elizabeth phrase in Darcy's initial judgement underestimates her?' - answer 'She is tolerable.'
findings.truth: The phrase is Darcy's, about Elizabeth. On a plain reading the question hands the line to the wrong speaker.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.3: '"She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me"' (Darcy).

findings.claim: 'Which Mrs Bennet stage direction captures her obvious excitement ...'
findings.truth: A novel has no stage directions. 'Quite in the fidgets' is narration.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.53: 'Mrs. Bennet was quite in the fidgets.'

findings.claim: Key themes of Pride and Prejudice with exam strategy for Eduqas Component 2 Section B.
findings.truth: Board name plus a banned paper/section code, in the field shown on every browse card.
findings.evidence: House rule and CHECK_PROMPT banned-string list.

findings.claim: You will be assessed against ... AO1 ..., AO2 ..., AO3 ..., and AO4 (accurate written expression). Check your exam board's specimen paper for exact mark weightings and timings.
findings.truth: AO4 is NOT assessed on the 19th-century prose question. The section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only, for 40 marks, and about 50 minutes is the sensible allowance. The 'check the specimen paper' line also dodged facts the lesson should state.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2: 'Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.' AO4 is assessed in Section A of the same component and in Component 1 Section A.

findings.claim: Key Fact: 'GCSE English Literature responses are assessed against four AOs ... Top-band responses embed all four within every paragraph.'
findings.truth: On this question only three are marked. Telling students to spend effort on AO4 here wastes time that earns nothing.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2: 'Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.'

findings.claim: For the Eduqas exam, embed AO1-AO4 within every paragraph
findings.truth: Board named, and AO4 is not assessed on this question.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2.

findings.claim: For the 40-mark Eduqas question, aim for 4-5 paragraphs.
findings.truth: The mark total is right; only the board name must go.
findings.evidence: House rule.

findings.claim: 'How many assessment objectives does the Eduqas 19th-century prose question assess?' with correct=2 -> 'Four (AO1, AO2, AO3, AO4)'.
findings.truth: Three (AO1, AO2, AO3). The key marked the true answer wrong and taught the false one. Stem also names the board.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2: 'Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.'

findings.claim: Glossary 'assessment objectives': '... identified as AO1, AO2, AO3, and AO4 by Eduqas.'
findings.truth: Board must not be named.
findings.evidence: House rule.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer 'Blind, partial, prejudiced, absurd.'
findings.truth: A bare comma list is rejected by the house validator. The quotation is kept but wrapped in a sentence. The wording itself is correct (ch.36).
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.36: 'she had been blind, partial, prejudiced, absurd.'

findings.claim: Every practice question is labelled 'Extract Analysis' and several say 'Read the extract' or 'Write about the extract', but no extract is printed with the question.
findings.truth: The real question does print an extract. The lessons cannot, so students meet a task they cannot fully attempt. Not a factual error; flagged for the practice-format backlog, no edit made.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2: Section B is 'a source based response'.

findings.claim: Mr Bennet 'has spent twenty years retreating into his library'; and 'Her father calls her the most sensible of his daughters'.
findings.truth: Austen gives 'three-and-twenty years' of marriage (ch.1), and Mr Bennet's actual praise is that Lizzy 'has something more of quickness than her sisters'. Both are loose paraphrases rather than errors, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.1.

findings.claim: Punctuation inside several quotations differs from the Gutenberg text: 'tolerable, but' (text: 'tolerable: but'), 'I am not romantic, you know;' (text: full stop), 'something more substantial, in the improvement' (text: no comma), Mary's 'ourselves, vanity' (text: semicolon).
findings.truth: These are edition variants, not misquotations. Wording, speaker and chapter are right in every case. No edit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch.3, ch.22, ch.8, ch.5.

summary: Eight lessons checked against the Gutenberg text and the Eduqas C720QS specification. Five misattributed quotations (Mr Bennet's and Mr Collins's lines given to Darcy and Mrs Bennet, Elizabeth's accusation given to Darcy, her refusal addressed to Jane), one fabricated clause, an AO4 claim on a question that carries no SPaG marks with a knowledge check keyed to the wrong answer, and every one of the 48 practice questions labelled 20 marks instead of 40.
